list.listitem: In any pregnant woman >20 weeks gestation with hypertension, obtain hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets, AST, ALT, LDH, creatinine, 24-hour urine for protein and uric acid, as well as a complete fetal ultrasound and NST to evaluate for HELLP syndrome. C
Standard treatment for HELLP syndrome is delivery of the fetus. A
Early diagnosis and active treatment with assistance from perinatologists for severe or pre-term HELLP syndrome is the only means to prevent worsening fetal and maternal morbidity and mortality. C
Steroids have not been shown to prevent maternal complications, though they decrease hospital length of stay. B

In gestations <34 weeks, if maternal condition is stable and there is no abdominal pain, blurred vision, headache, or signs of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), delivery can be delayed by 24 hours to administer steroids to increase fetal lung maturity. A

background.definition: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets (HELLP) syndrome is a severe form of preeclampsia. Preeclampsia is a multi-system disease of pregnancy associated with an increase in blood pressure and associated with increased perinatal and maternal morbidity and mortality. HELLP is classified into three classes. Class 1: platelet nadir <50,000; class 2: platelet nadir >50,000 and <100,000; and class 3: platelet nadir >100,000 and <150,000.

list.listitem: HELLP syndrome occurs in 0.2% to 0.8% of all pregnancies.
80% of women with HELLP syndrome present in the antepartum period.
38% of women with HELLP syndrome have an infant with intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR).

HELLP syndrome is highly associated with adverse neonatal outcomes, including respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) (74% of all NICU admissions from HELLP), fetal thrombocytopenia (38%), intracranial hemorrhage (31% with abnormal doppler, 6% with normal doppler), and fetal and neonatal demise (22% with abnormal doppler findings, 10% with normal doppler).
As with preeclampsia, the etiology and pathogenesis of HELLP syndrome is not completely understood.
Antiphospholipid antibodies have not been shown to be a major cause of HELLP syndrome.
Abnormal development of an ischemic placenta with a high-resistance vasculature cannot deliver an adequate blood supply to the fetoplacental unit.
Dysfunctional endothelial cells produce altered quantities of vasoactive mediators, which lead to vasoconstriction.
An imbalance in circulating angiogenic factors is emerging as a prominent mechanism that mediates the endothelial dysfunction and the clinical signs and symptoms of preeclampsia.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: First-degree relatives with chronic HTN or hyperlipidemia

list.listitem: Low-dose aspirin has not been shown to prevent preeclampsia in women at low risk, and therefore is not recommended. A

A meta-analysis of 14 high-quality studies found that aspirin was effective for high-risk women (previous preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, renal disease, and extreme age at conception). Based on these data, the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends the use of low-dose (81 mg) aspirin as preventive medication after 12 weeks gestation in women at high risk for preeclampsia.A
Calcium supplementation does not prevent preeclampsia in healthy nulliparous women. A
Vitamins C and E do not prevent preeclampsia. B
The USPSTF recommends screening for preeclampsia with blood pressure measurements throughout pregnancy. B
Any patient over 20 weeks gestation presenting with hypertension with or without headache, abdominal pain, visual disturbance, or vomiting should be evaluated for preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome. C
Admission lab tests include hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets, AST, ALT, LDH, creatinine, 24-hour urine for protein, and uric acid. C
Fetal testing includes continuous NST, ultrasound (for estimated fetal weight and fetal survey), BPP, and uterine artery doppler. C

Differential.Differential_Features: No hypertension, only platelets affected, lack of response to dexamethasone in 12 to 24 hours
No hypertension, no end organ effect

list.listitem: Any patient over 20 weeks gestation with elevated blood pressure and/or with cerebral or visual disturbances, epigastric or right upper-quadrant (RUQ) pain, fetal growth restriction, or headache needs to be screened urgently for preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome.
Clinical symptoms of headache and abdominal pain are independent and important components of worsening disease.
A past medical history of preeclampsia/HELLP, any form of chronic hypertension, or kidney disease places a patient at higher risk of HELLP.
Pulmonary edema or cyanosis can, in rare cases, be the presenting symptom of late HELLP syndrome and requires emergent delivery.

Sometimes HELLP syndrome presents in the postpartum period, so any patient who has a low platelet count or hypertension during delivery, or develops them postpartum, should also undergo laboratory screening.
Although various laboratory tests may be useful in the management of women with preeclampsia, to date there is no reliable predictive test for preeclampsia.

Order a hemoglobin/hematocrit and platelet count to detect evidence of hemolysis and thrombocytopenia. In a retrospective analysis of 545 patients with HELLP, there was a correlation between the rate of platelet drop and severity of disease. Patients who developed class 1 or 2 HELLP syndrome exhibited more rapid deterioration in platelet count than those with class 3 (45,000-50,000/microliter/day vs. 30,000/microliter/day). Women with platelets counts under 60,000/microliter had a significantly higher incidence of fetuses with intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) than women with higher platelet counts (p <0.002).

Elevations in AST, ALT, and/or LDH are necessary for the diagnosis of HELLP and can help predict severity; elevated values on admission increased the post-test probability of class 1 HELLP at 71%, 78%, and 74%, respectively, and 90% if all three were elevated.

A 24-hour urine for protein should be collected on all pregnant women with hypertension regardless of the urine dipstick. The positive predictive value (PPV) of a urine dipstick is 65% and of a 24-hour urine protein is 94%; negative predictive value (NPV) of urine dipstick is 73% and of 24-hour urine is 84%. Therefore a urine protein >300 mg/24 h is a good indicator of preeclampsia. It is, however, a poor indicator of adverse outcomes.
Creatinine over 0.6 in pregnancy is an indicator of kidney disfunction and should be watched carefully.

A serum uric acid level has been used in women with preeclampsia to predict risk of eclampsia; a positive test result (i.e., uric acid greater than or equal to a 350 micromol/L) predicted eclampsia with a positive likelihood ratio (LR) of 2.1 (95% CI, 1.4-3.5), while a negative test result had a negative LR of 0.38 (95% CI, 0.18-0.81). Serum uric acid, however, is a poor predictor of maternal and fetal complications in women with preeclampsia.

Doppler flow velocimetry of the uterine artery, umbilical artery, and fetal circulation demonstrated very high sensitivity (83%) and specificity (80%) in predicting adverse outcome in growth retarded fetuses but not in normal weight fetuses (NPV 56%).

Laboratory testing frequency depends on the severity of the case. In slowly progressive cases and recovering postpartum patients, every 24 hours is adequate. For patients in labor who are not in severe condition or rapidly progressing, test every 12 hours. For the rapidly progressive HELLP patient in labor, with concerning symptoms or change in condition, test every 6 hours.
Any patient over 20 weeks gestation presenting with hypertension with or without headache, abdominal pain, visual disturbance, or vomiting should be evaluated for preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome.

Admission labs include hemoglobin, hematocrit, platelets, AST, ALT, LDH, creatinine, 24-hour urine for protein, and uric acid. Fetal testing includes continuous nonstress test, ultrasound for estimated fetal weight and to evaluate for intrauterine growth retardation, a fetal survey, biophysical profile, and uterine artery doppler.
If visual disturbance, RUQ pain, severe headache, renal damage, or any significantly abnormal laboratory tests present, admit immediately and consider imminent delivery after 36 weeks.

Delivery of the fetus and all placental tissues is the mainstay of treatment after 34 weeks gestation. If stable, treatment with corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity for 24 hours prior to delivery is advised for gestations under 34 weeks. A
Magnesium sulfate should be given to all patients meeting the criteria of HELLP syndrome and continued for 24 hours postpartum. A

Steroid treatment for thrombocytopenia antepartum or postpartum has not been shown to decrease maternal morbidity and mortality. Treatment with dexamethasone does increase platelet count and improves urinary and liver parameters, decreasing overall hospital length of stay. B
Patients with diastolic blood pressures over 105 to 110 should be started on hydralazine or labetolol. C

Magnesium sulfate should be used for the prevention and treatment of seizures in women with severe preeclampsia or eclampsia. Consider 4g IV loading dose for over 10 minutes and 2 g/h IV drip if no renal insufficiency presents. Check Mg levels every 6 hours. Magnesium maintenance dose should be decreased by 50% to prevent magnesium toxicity when creatinine is high. If magnesium sulphate is given, it should be continued for 24 hours following delivery. RCTs have shown that magnesium is more effective than both phenytoin and dilantin for prevention of seizures in eclampsia.
Daily calcium supplementation has not been shown to prevent preeclampsia, and therefore is not recommended.

Low-dose aspirin has not been shown to prevent preeclampsia in women at low risk, and therefore is not recommended. There is evidence of benefit in high-risk patients, so consider administering it to them.

Antihypertensive therapy (with either hydralazine 5 mg IV every 20 minutes or labetalol 10 to 20 mg IVP repeating every 20 minutes for a maximum of 300 mg as needed) should be used for treatment of diastolic blood pressure over 105 to 110 mm Hg. Antihypertensive medication can be required for up to 3 months postpartum.

There is insufficient evidence to recommend adjunctive steroid use in HELLP syndrome to decrease maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity. Women given dexamethasone (5 mg PO every 6 hours x 48 hours), however, fared significantly better for: oliguria, mean arterial pressure, mean increase in platelet count, mean increase in urinary output, and liver enzyme elevations. There was a decrease in overall hospital length of stay.

If the pregnancy is <34 weeks gestation and the maternal condition is not rapidly worsening, and there is no abdominal pain, blurred vision, headache, or signs of diffuse intravascular coagulopathy, steroids (betamethasone 12 mg IM every 24 hours x 2 or 6 mg IM every 12 hours x 4 OR dexamethasone 6 mg IM every 12 hours x 4) for fetal lung maturity can be administered for 24 hours prior to delivery.

A systematic review of 15 RCTs with 821 women concluded that steroids had an uncertain effect on maternal death (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.25 to 2.38), pulmonar edema (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.23 to 2.09), the need for dialysis (RR 3.0, 95% CI 0.13 to 70.78) or perinatal death (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.97).
Cesarian section is indicated as the primary mode of delivery in cases where there is end organ failure, rapidly progressive preeclampsia, DIC, severe hypertension, or far from delivery.
Spinal anesthesia is contraindicated when the platelet count is less than 100,000.

Delivery of the fetus and all placental tissues is the mainstay of treatment after 34 weeks gestation. If stable, treatment with steroids for fetal lung maturity for 24 hours prior to delivery is advised for gestations under 34 weeks.
Invasive hemodynamic monitoring should be considered in preeclamptic women with severe cardiac disease, renal disease, refractory hypertension, pulmonary edema, or unexplained oliguria.
Antihypertensive medication may need to be continued for 3 months postpartum.
Any patient with hypertension and proteinuria persisting over 6 weeks postpartum should be further evaluated for renal disease.

The management of a woman with severe preeclampsia remote from term is best accomplished in a tertiary care setting or in consultation with an obstetrician/gynecologist with training, experience, and demonstrated competence in the management of high-risk pregnancies, such as a maternal/fetal medicine subspecialist.
Factors associated with HELLP syndrome that confer significantly increased morbidity and mortality include multiorgan dysfunction syndrome, DIC, and Apgar scores <5 at 1 minute (CB). B
More rapid rate of platelet drop and elevations in AST, ALT, and/or LDH help predict severity of HELLP. B
The most common cause for mortality among women with preeclampsia is HELLP syndrome. B

A systematic review of 11 cohort studies with 6333 women found associations between HELLP syndrome and acute kidney injury (OR 4.9, 95% CI 3.3-7.2), maternal death (OR 3.7, 95% CI 1.7-8.0), and fetal mortality (OR 1.56 95% CI 1.45-2.11).

Inpatient observation should continue until hemolysis, low platelet counts, liver enzymes, and blood pressure begin to normalize or are reasonably controlled. Most women with severe preeclampsia stay for a minimum of 4 days postpartum. C
